title: ChatGPT
seoTitle: Design a Chat Assistant Like ChatGPT
description: Design ChatGPT — conversations with an LLM, streaming token responses, conversation history, GPU capacity management, and rate limiting.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is ChatGPT?
blocks.text: ChatGPT is a conversational assistant. Users send messages in a chat, and a large language model (LLM) generates a reply that streams back token by token.

items: Users should be able to start a conversation and send messages.
Responses should stream back to the user as they are generated.
Users should be able to view and continue past conversations.
File uploads, tools, image generation, and voice.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Time to first token should be low (< 1s at normal load).
The system should scale to 100M weekly users and use expensive GPU capacity efficiently.
Conversations must be durable — a user's history should never disappear.
The system should degrade gracefully under overload (queue or rate limit rather than fall over).

blocks.text: Most of the system is a fairly standard chat app. What's unusual is the **inference tier**: requests are long-running (seconds to minutes), extremely expensive, and capacity-constrained by GPUs. We'll focus the deep dives there.

items: **User**: with a plan tier that determines limits.
**Conversation**: an ordered list of messages with a title.

blocks.text: 1) Users should be able to send messages
The **Chat Service** stores the user's message, builds the prompt from the conversation history (truncated or summarised to fit the model's context window), and sends it to the **Inference Service**.
2) Responses should stream back as they are generated

The model generates one token at a time. Rather than waiting for the full answer, the Inference Service streams tokens to the Chat Service, which forwards them to the client over **Server-Sent Events**. The response is a single long-lived HTTP response, so SSE fits naturally — no bidirectional WebSocket needed.
When generation completes, the full assistant message is written to the database.
3) Users should be able to view past conversations

Conversations and messages are stored in a database keyed by `userId` / `conversationId`. A wide-column or document store (e.g. DynamoDB with partition key `conversationId`, sort key `messageTs`) scales well for this append-heavy, read-by-conversation pattern.
1) How do we use scarce GPU capacity efficiently?

blocks.title: One request per GPU at a time

approach.text: Route each request to a free GPU worker, which processes it to completion before taking another.

challenges.text: GPUs are memory-bandwidth bound during generation; serving one sequence at a time leaves most of the compute idle and throughput terrible.

approach.text: Inference servers batch many concurrent requests together and use **continuous (in-flight) batching**: new requests join the batch as others finish, at token granularity. Combined with a KV cache for attention state, this multiplies throughput per GPU. A router sends requests to the replica with available KV-cache capacity.

challenges.text: Larger batches raise per-token latency, so batch size is tuned against latency SLOs. Long prompts consume lots of cache memory and must be scheduled carefully.

blocks.text: 2) What happens when demand exceeds GPU capacity?

blocks.title: Accept everything and let latency grow

approach.text: Send every request to inference and hope capacity holds.

challenges.text: Queues grow unbounded, requests time out after users have waited a long time, and the system thrashes.

blocks.title: Admission control: rate limits, priority queues and load shedding

approach.text: Enforce per-user rate limits by plan (token bucket on messages and on tokens per minute). Put admitted requests into **priority queues** (paid tiers first) in front of the inference router with a bounded wait; when the queue is full or the expected wait exceeds a threshold, return a friendly "at capacity" error immediately. Optionally fall back to a smaller, cheaper model under pressure.

challenges.text: Requires accurate capacity signals (queue depth, KV-cache utilisation) and careful UX for degraded responses.

blocks.text: 3) What if the user's connection drops mid-stream?

blocks.title: Tie generation to the HTTP connection

approach.text: If the client disconnects, cancel generation and discard the partial response.

challenges.text: Mobile users lose answers constantly, and wasted GPU work is thrown away.

approach.text: Generation writes tokens to a short-lived stream (e.g. Redis Stream keyed by messageId) and persists the final message to the database. The SSE handler reads from that stream. A reconnecting client calls `GET /messages/:id/stream?offset=N` and resumes from where it left off; if generation already finished, it simply reads the stored message.

challenges.text: More moving parts; streams need TTLs, and explicit "stop generating" requests must still cancel the inference job to save GPU time.

blocks.title: Pattern: Managing Long Running Tasks
blocks.text: LLM responses can take a minute. Separating the work (generation) from the client connection (delivery) is what makes them resilient.

quiz.question: Why is SSE a natural fit for streaming LLM responses?
options: Traffic during generation is one-way, server to client, over a single response
quiz.explanation: The client sends one request and receives a stream of tokens back.

quiz.question: What does continuous batching improve?
options: GPU throughput by adding and removing requests from the batch at token granularity
quiz.explanation: Keeping the batch full uses GPU compute that single-request serving leaves idle.

quiz.question: How should the system behave when GPU demand exceeds capacity?
options: Rate limit, queue with priorities and shed load with a fast error
quiz.explanation: Admission control keeps latency bounded instead of letting everything time out.

quiz.question: How can a client resume a response after its connection drops?
options: Generation writes to a stream the client can resume from an offset
quiz.explanation: Decoupling generation from delivery lets clients reconnect without losing or regenerating work.
